title: Travers Smith launches innovative open sourced YCNBot
author: Travers Smith

kp.k: Open-source chatbot offers enterprise access to generative AI
kp.d: The press release announces YCNBot, developed by Travers Smith's Legal Technology team in collaboration with 273 Ventures. Available free under an open-source licence, it lets law firms and other organisations replace consumer-facing ChatGPT with a chatbot connected to Microsoft and OpenAI enterprise APIs. The firm presents this as a safer deployment approach with enhanced compliance, security and data-privacy controls for confidential and sensitive information; these are the firm's claims, not reported independent findings.
qs: Travers Smith LLP has launched its latest open source project, YCNBot, in collaboration with 273 Ventures.

Created by the firm's pioneering Legal Technology team, YCNBot (which stands for Your Company Name e.g. TSBot), is available for anyone to download and deploy free of charge through an open source license, enabling, law firms and other organisations to replace the consumer facing ChatGPT with a chat-bot that plugs into Enterprise API's of Microsoft and OpenAI.
This ensures essential enhanced controls around compliance, security and data privacy for businesses which handles confidential, sensitive and Personal Identifiable Information (PII).

kp.k: Internal experimentation explicitly excludes direct client work
kp.d: As of the 24 May 2023 release, the firm reports rolling out its implementation, TSBot, across Travers Smith. Lawyers and business services employees are encouraged to learn, experiment and provide feedback, while direct client work is expressly excluded. The announced deployment therefore concerns internal learning rather than AI delivery of client legal services.
qs: TSBot has been rolled out across at Travers Smith, with lawyers and business services employees encouraged to learn, experiment, and provide feedback to the Legal Technology team.
It will not be used for any direct client work.

kp.k: Development combines external collaboration with evolving safeguards
kp.d: Travers Smith reports developing the platform with guidance and support from 273 Ventures, led by Mike Bommarito and Dan Katz. The release distinguishes existing features—enhanced privacy, feedback submission and administrative analytics—from planned continued development incorporating further safeguards proposed by regulators.
qs: Travers Smith developed the platform with guidance and support from 273 Ventures, led by Mike Bommarito and Dan Katz.
The two companies will continue to develop and enhance YCNBot, building in further safeguards proposed by regulators as the technology continues to evolve.
The latest version includes enhanced privacy, the ability to submit feedback, and an analytics view for administrative users.

kp.k: Technology leadership frames deployment as research and client dialogue
kp.d: Chief Technology Officer Oliver Bethell describes the Legal Technology and AI team's work as research into how the technology could affect future legal services, rather than presenting measured changes in legal work. He also reports that YCNBot has prompted client conversations about generative AI's opportunities and risks.
qs: Our team of Legal Technology and AI experts are focussed on research and development to understand how this incredible new technology could impact legal services in the future.
YCNBot has been a fantastic catalyst for conversations with our clients, to understand how they are viewing the opportunities and risks of generative AI.

kp.k: Generative AI predicted consequential, but adoption requires caution
kp.d: Head of Legal Technology Shawn Curran predicts a critical future role for generative AI in the industry while stressing caution. He characterises YCNBot as a temporary response to an evolving enterprise chatbot market, intended to enable business learning in a secure setting. His statements express expectations and the project's rationale, not demonstrated productivity or market outcomes.
qs: There is no doubt Generative AI is here to stay and will play a critical role in our industry in the years ahead, but we do recognise the need to proceed with caution.

There is a huge business potential in this emerging technology but whilst the enterprise chatbot market evolves, it was essential for us to ensure we could access the same technology in a secure setting for businesses which is why we developed and open sourced YCNBot.
This has allowed us to fill the gap temporarily, enabling companies to interact with the technology for learning purposes in the safest possible way available at this time.

kp.k: Existing legal technology targets document review and closing workflows
kp.d: The release places YCNBot alongside work combining lawyers and technology experts. It reports that Etatonna labels contract concepts for automated document review and won a CogX award in 2022, while a DocuSign-based automated eSignature closing process delivered over 400 closings at no additional cost to clients. It also identifies open-sourcing legal technology, including Etatonna, as a means of encouraging legal-market collaboration. These are reported prior initiatives, not outcomes attributed to YCNBot.
qs: Launched Etatonna, the first legal industry data labelling AI platform, which labels concepts in contracts for the purpose of automated document review, which won a CogX award in 2022.
Automated eSignature closing process using DocuSign, delivering over 400 closings, at no additional cost to clients.
Open-sourcing Travers Smith’s legal technology, including Etatonna, to inspire collaboration in the legal market.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Travers Smith claims YCNBot enables safer organisational access to generative AI through enterprise APIs and enhanced controls.
pts.d: The firm's press release describes YCNBot as a free, open-source alternative interface to consumer-facing ChatGPT, developed with 273 Ventures. It claims that connecting to Microsoft and OpenAI enterprise APIs provides enhanced compliance, security and privacy controls for organisations handling confidential and sensitive information. This is a claim about enabling controlled adoption and experimentation, not demonstrated improvements in client legal work.

pts.k: Shawn Curran predicts a lasting, critical role for generative AI in the legal industry, while presenting YCNBot as an interim learning tool.
pts.d: Travers Smith's Head of Legal Technology asserts that generative AI has substantial business potential and will be important to the industry in the years ahead. He does not specify particular changes in staffing, pricing, productivity or legal-service delivery. His immediate claim is that YCNBot temporarily fills a gap while the enterprise chatbot market develops, allowing businesses to learn about the technology in a secure setting.

pts.k: Oliver Bethell reports that YCNBot has facilitated client discussions about generative AI opportunities and risks.
pts.d: The firm's Chief Technology Officer describes an existing effect on client engagement and research, rather than a measured transformation of legal services. Separately, the firm describes its Etatonna platform as labelling concepts in contracts for automated document review, identifying another concrete legal-AI application without quantifying its performance.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source relies on the firm's deployment experience, product descriptions and executives' assessments, not measured legal-service outcomes.
pts.d: For YCNBot, the release offers the reported firm-wide rollout, enterprise API architecture and specific privacy, feedback and administrative features as support for its adoption and safety claims. Bethell's client-engagement claim rests on reported experience. Curran's industry prediction is an executive assessment without supporting data or a specified forecasting method. The release provides no comparative security testing, model benchmarks, quantified productivity gains or client-work results. Etatonna's launch and 2022 award are cited as background credentials, not evidence of YCNBot's effectiveness.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The May 2023 release describes an already-deployed learning tool, explicitly excludes direct client work and leaves the broader industry forecast undated.
pts.d: As of 24 May 2023, YCNBot had launched and Travers Smith's version had been rolled out internally. Its immediate use was learning and experimentation, with an explicit prohibition on direct client work. Curran qualifies the claimed safety relative to what was available at that time and calls the solution temporary while enterprise chatbots evolve. His prediction concerns 'the years ahead' without a deadline. Travers Smith and 273 Ventures also state an intention to continue development and incorporate further regulator-proposed safeguards.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Immediate beneficiaries are lawyers, business-services staff and organisations seeking controlled AI experimentation; clients are involved through discussion rather than direct AI-assisted work.
pts.d: Travers Smith employees receive internal access for learning and feedback. Other law firms and organisations can download and deploy the open-source software without a licence charge, particularly where confidentiality and personal information create adoption concerns. Administrative users receive an analytics view, and the Legal Technology team receives user feedback. Clients are described as participants in conversations about opportunities and risks, not recipients of direct YCNBot-produced legal work. Curran's longer-term prediction concerns the legal industry generally, without distinguishing particular practice areas or firm sizes.
